extraction_notes.note: The 'Idea of the proof' of Lemma 4.1 is a proof sketch; the sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal but rigor is not allowed on proof nodes, so it is left off and only the alternative flag on its proves edge marks it.
Remark environments that state standard Taylor bounds for sqrt(1-x^2); retyped claim with origin external (standard, uncited) rather than remark.

The noise-model sentences both define M_sigma and state the sampling assumption; typed definition, and the labelled enumerated item (Section 2.1, restated in Section 3) is kept as the assumption node.
Subsection 8.2.2 is a standalone derivation of the simplified condition on a1, a2 used in the proof of Claim 4; no stated result to prove, so it is a remark used by that proof.

Lemma statements of Section 9.1.1 say 'let the conditions of Lemma X hold' and 'as defined in (eq) in the proof of Lemma X'; these refer to hypotheses and notation, not to the truth of X, and are marked mention (otherwise they close result cycles with the proofs that use them).
The proof cites Theorem \ref{thm:vector_LPR}, a label absent from this source (presumably a result of the cited vector-valued regression paper); two tikz roadmap figures were removed from the source.

Proof of Lemma 4.2 is an enumerated list of claims cited later by number; cited items are Level-1 claims nested in the proof, their separate 'Proof of Claim' paragraphs (and Section 8.2.1) are proof nodes.

nodes.statement: The reach of a subset $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^D$, is the largest $\tau$ \emph{(}possibly $\infty$\emph{)} such that for any $x\in\mathbb{R}^D$ that maintains $dist(A,x)\leq \tau$, there exists a unique point $P_A(x)\in A$, nearest to $x$.
nodes.name: Reach
differentia: for any $x\in\mathbb{R}^D$ that maintains $dist(A,x)\leq \tau$, there exists a unique point $P_A(x)\in A$, nearest to $x$
nodes.label: def:reach

nodes.name: Tubular neighborhood $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ and noise model
nodes.statement_short: Samples are drawn i.i.d. uniformly from the open $\sigma$-tubular neighborhood $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ of $\mathcal{M}$.

nodes.statement: \mathcal{M}_\sigma \stackrel{\bigtriangleup}{=} \{q\in \mathbb{R}^D ~|~ dist(q, \mathcal{M}) < \sigma \} ,

nodes.label: eq:Msigma

nodes.name: Local chart $\varphi_p$ over the tangent space
nodes.statement_short: Near $p$, $\mathcal{M}$ is the graph $\varphi_p(x)=p+(x,\phi_p(x))$ of a function from the tangent space to its normal space.

nodes.statement: \varphi_p:W_{T_p\mathcal{M}}\to \mathcal{M}
nodes.name: Equation (2) [eq:LocalChart_clean]
nodes.label: eq:LocalChart_clean

nodes.statement: \varphi_p(x) = p+(x,\phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} ,
nodes.name: Equation (3) [eq:phi_def_clean]
nodes.label: eq:phi_def_clean

nodes.name: Graph $\Gamma_{\phi_p, W_p}$ of $\phi_p$

nodes.statement: \Gamma_{\phi_p, W_p} \stackrel{\bigtriangleup}{=} \{p + (x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} | x\in W_{T_p\mathcal{M}} \} .
nodes.name: Equation (4) [eq:FunctionGraph_init]
nodes.label: eq:FunctionGraph_init

nodes.name: Region of interest $U_{\textrm{ROI}}$
nodes.statement_short: The ROI is the set of samples within distance $\sqrt{\sigma\tau}$ of $r$; $N$ is their number.

nodes.statement: U_{\textrm{ROI}} = {\{r_i|\operatorname{dist}(r_i,r)<\sqrt{\sigma\tau}\}} ,
nodes.name: Equation (5) [eq:ROI_clean]
nodes.label: eq:ROI_clean

nodes.name: Step 1 minimization of $J_1$ (local coordinate system)
nodes.statement_short: Find an origin $q$ and $d$-plane $H$ minimizing the mean squared distance of ROI samples to $q+H$, with $r-q\perp H$ and $\|r-q\|<2\sigma$.

nodes.statement: J_1(r; q, H) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{r_i\in U_{\textrm{ROI}}} \operatorname{dist}^2 (r_i - q,H)
nodes.name: Equation (6) [eq:J1_clean]
nodes.label: eq:J1_clean

nodes.name: Minimizers $q^*(r), H^*(r)$

nodes.statement: q^*(r), H^*(r) = \arg\!\min_{\substack{ q, H \\ r-q \perp H \\ \|r- q\|<2\sigma}} J_1(r; q, H)
nodes.name: Equation (7) [eq:argmin1_clean]
nodes.label: eq:argmin1_clean

nodes.statement: \caption{Step 1: Find an initial coordinate system} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Statex {\bfseries Input:}\begin{tabular}[t]{ll} $\{r_i\}_{i=1}^n\subset \mathcal{M}_\sigma$ & noisy samples of a $d$ dimensional manifold $ \mathcal{M} $.\\ $r\in \mathcal{M}_\sigma$ & a point in a tubular neighborhood of $\mathcal{M}$. \end{tabular} \Statex {\bfseries Output:}\begin{tabular}[t]{ll} $q^*$ & crude estimation of $p = P_{\mathcal{M}}(r)$.\\ $H^*$ & estimation of $T_p\mathcal{M}$.\\ \end{tabular} \State Disregard points outside of $U_{\textrm{ROI}}$. \State Find $q^*, H^*$ minimizing \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} subject to $\norm{q^* - r}<2\sigma$ and $r - q^* \perp H^*$. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.name: Step 1: Find an initial coordinate system
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the ROI and solve the constrained minimization of $J_1$ for a crude origin $q^*$ and tangent estimate $H^*$.
input: noisy samples of a $d$ dimensional manifold $ \mathcal{M} $.
a point in a tubular neighborhood of $\mathcal{M}$.
nodes.label: alg:alg1_clean

nodes.statement: Disregard points outside of $U_{\textrm{ROI}}$.
nodes.name: Disregard points outside of $U_{\textrm{ROI}}$.

nodes.statement: Find $q^*, H^*$ minimizing \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} subject to $\norm{q^* - r}<2\sigma$ and $r - q^* \perp H^*$.
nodes.name: Find $q^*, H^*$ minimizing \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} subject
Local polynomial regression $J_2$
nodes.statement_short: Fit a degree-$(k-1)$ polynomial from $H$ to $H^\perp$ by least squares to samples whose projection lies within bandwidth $\epsilon_n$.

nodes.statement: J_2(\pi ~|~ q, H) = \frac{1}{N_{q, H}}\sum_{r_i \in U_{\textrm{ROI}}^n} \norm{r_i - (x_i, \pi(x_i))_H}^2 ,
nodes.name: Equation (8) [eq:Step2_clean]
nodes.label: eq:Step2_clean

nodes.statement: U_{\textrm{ROI}}^n(q,H) = {\{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}~|~\norm{x_i}<\epsilon_n\}} ,
nodes.name: Equation (9) [eq:ROI_ell_clean]
nodes.label: eq:ROI_ell_clean

nodes.name: Local polynomial regression estimate $\pi^*_{q,H}$

nodes.statement: \pi^*_{q, H} = \arg\!\min_{\pi\in \Pi_{k-1}^{d\mapsto D}} J_2(\pi ~|~ q, H) .
nodes.name: Equation (10) [eq:argmin2_clean]
nodes.label: eq:argmin2_clean

nodes.name: Bandwidth decay $\epsilon_n \sim n^{-1/(2k+1)}$

nodes.statement: 0<\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}n^{1/(2k+1)}\cdot \epsilon_n < \infty .
nodes.name: Equation (11) [eq:bandwidthDecay_clean]
nodes.label: eq:bandwidthDecay_clean

nodes.statement:
For simplicity of notations, we abuse the definition of $ \pi^*_{q, H}$ in \eqref{eq:argmin2_clean}, and define
\begin{equation} \pi^*_{q, H} = \mbox{Algorithm 2 of \cite{aizenbud2021VectorEstimation}} (x_i,y_i),
\end{equation}
where $y_i$ are the projection of $r_i-q$ onto $H^\perp$.
nodes.name: $\pi^*_{q,H}$ via the median-trick estimator
nodes.statement_short: Redefine $\pi^*_{q,H}$ as the output of the median-trick local polynomial estimator (Algorithm 2 of the cited work).

nodes.statement: \pi^*_{q, H} = \mbox{Algorithm 2 of \cite{aizenbud2021VectorEstimation}} (x_i,y_i),
nodes.name: Equation (12) [eq:pi_star_median_trick]
nodes.label: eq:pi_star_median_trick

nodes.statement: For simplicity of presentation, throughout the paper when we write $\partial \pi^*_{q, H}$ or $\mathcal{D}_{\pi^*_{q_\ell,H_{\ell}}}$ what we actually mean is the estimate of the derivative rather than the derivative of $\pi^*_{q, H}$.
nodes.name: Derivative notation for $\pi^*$

nodes.statement: We begin by setting $q_{-1} = q^*$ (a crude approximation of a point on the manifold) and $H_0 = H^*$ (the initial tangent estimate) resulting from Algorithm \ref{alg:alg1_clean}.
nodes.name: Initialization $q_{-1}$, $H_0$

nodes.statement: Then, in order to have the origin $q$ closer to $\mathcal{M}$ we begin by updating $q_0 = q_{-1} + (0, \pi^*_{q_{-1}, H_0}(0))_{H_0}$.
nodes.name: First origin update $q_0$

nodes.statement: Explicitly, in iteration $\ell$, we define $H_{\ell+1}$ to be the subspace coinciding with $ \mathrm{Im}(\mathcal{D}_{\pi^*_{q_{\ell}, H_{\ell}}}[0]) $ the image of the differential of $(\textrm{Id},\pi^*_{q_{\ell},H_{\ell}}):\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^D$ at $ 0 $ (i.e., the tangent to the graph of $ \pi^*_{q_{\ell  }, H_{\ell }} $).
nodes.name: Tangent update $H_{\ell+1}$
nodes.statement_short: $H_{\ell+1}$ is the image of the differential at 0 of the graph map of the regression estimate $\pi^*_{q_\ell,H_\ell}$.

nodes.name: Local function $f_\ell$ over $H_\ell$

nodes.statement: f_{\ell}:\mathbb{R}^d\simeq H_\ell \to \mathbb{R}^{D-d} \simeq H_\ell ^\perp .
nodes.name: Equation (13)

nodes.statement:
That is, we define a local patch of the manifold through the graph 
\begin{equation} \Gamma_{f_\ell, q_\ell, H_\ell} = \{q_\ell + (x, f_\ell(x))_{H_\ell} | x\in B_{H_\ell}(0,\rho) \}\subset\mathcal{M},   
\end{equation}
where $\rho$ is some radius where this function is defined (see Lemma \ref{lem:M_is_locally_a_fuinction_clean} for more details regarding the existence of such $\rho > 0$).

nodes.statement: \caption{Step 1: in practice} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State {\bfseries Input:} $\lbrace r_i \rbrace_{i=1}^N, r, \epsilon$ \State{\bfseries Output:}\begin{tabular}[t]{ll} $q$ - an $n$ dimensional vector \\ $U$ - an $n\times d$ matrix whose columns are $\lbrace u_j \rbrace_{j=1}^d$ \end{tabular} \Comment{$H = q + Span\lbrace u_j \rbrace_{j=1}^d$} \State define $R$ to be an $n\times N$ matrix whose columns are $r_i$ \State initialize $U$ with the first $d$ principal components of the spatially weighted PCA \State $q\leftarrow r$ \Repeat \State $q_{prev} = q$ \State $\tilde{R} = (R - repmat(q,1,N))\cdot \Theta$ \Comment{where $\Theta$ is an indicator for points in $U_{\textrm{ROI}}$} \State $X_{N\times d} = \tilde{R}^T U$ \Comment{find the representation of $r_i$ in $Col(U)$} \State define $\tilde{X}_{N\times (d+1)} = \left[(1,...,1)^T, X\right]$ \State solve $\tilde{X}^T\tilde{X}\alpha = \tilde{X}^T \tilde{R}^T$ for $\alpha \in M_{(d+1)\times n}$ \Comment{solving the LS minimization of $\tilde{X}\alpha \approx \tilde{R}^T$} \State $\tilde{q} = q + \alpha(1,:)^T$ \State $Q, \hat{R} = qr(\alpha(2:end, :)^T)$ \Comment{where $qr$ denotes the QR decomposition} \State $U \leftarrow Q$ \State $q = \tilde{q} + U U^T (r-\tilde{q})$ \Until {$\|q-q_{\text{prev}}\|<\epsilon$} \end{algorithmic}

nodes.statement: The proof can be described by the following three arguments which are proven in Lemmas \ref{lem:J1pTp_clean}, \ref{lem:J_1qH_clean}. \begin{enumerate} \item[Arg. 1:] Denote $p_r = P_{\mathcal{M}}(r)$. Then, since $r - p_r\perp T_{p_r}\mathcal{M} $ and $r\in\mathcal{M}_\sigma$, we have that $q = p_r$ along with $H= T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}$ are in the search space defined by the constraints of \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean}. \item[Arg. 2:] From Lemma \ref{lem:J1pTp_clean} it follows that for large enough $M = \tau/\sigma$ such that $ \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\tau}} + \frac{\sigma}{\tau} < \frac{1}{2} $ we have $J_1(r; p_r; T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}) \leq 50\cdot \sigma^2$. According to Assumption \ref{assume:noise} in Section \ref{sec:SamplingAssumptions}, we have that $M$ is large enough, and Lemma \ref{lem:J1pTp_clean} hold. Due to the definition of $q^*, H^*$ in \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean}, we achieve that $J_1(r; q^*, H^*) \leq 50 \cdot \sigma^2$ as well. \item[Arg. 3:] From Lemma \ref{lem:J_1qH_clean}, we have that for $\alpha = \sqrt{C_M/M}$, where $M = \frac{\tau}{\sigma}$, and $C_M$ is a constant the following holds: For any $\delta >0$ arbitrarily small there is $ N_{\delta} $ sufficiently large (independent of $\alpha$) such that for all $ n>N_{\delta} $, \textbf{all} pairs $(q, H)$ in the search space of \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} such that $\angle_{max}(H,T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}) > \alpha$, the score $J_1(r; q, H) \geq 100 \sigma^2 $ with probability of at least $1 - \delta$. \end{enumerate} Combining Arguments 2 and 3 we have that for $\alpha = \sqrt{C_M/M}$, where $M = \frac{\tau}{\sigma}$, and $C_M$ is a constant the following holds: For any $\delta>0$ arbitrarily small, there exists $ N_{\delta} $ (independent of $\alpha$) such that for all $ n > N_{\delta} $ \[\angle_{\max}(H^*, T_p\mathcal{M})\leq \alpha\] with probability of at least $ 1 - \delta $. Additionally, since the search space of \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} requires that $\|r-q^*\| <2\sigma$, we have that $\|p-q^*\|\leq 3\sigma$, and the proof is concluded.

nodes.statement_short: Three arguments: the true projection and tangent are feasible with $J_1\le 50\sigma^2$ (Lemma 4.1), while every plane tilted more than $\alpha$ scores $J_1\ge 100\sigma^2$ (Lemma 4.3).

nodes.statement:
The proof can be described by the following three arguments which are proven in Lemmas \ref{lem:J1pTp_clean}, \ref{lem:J_1qH_clean}.
\begin{enumerate}
nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement_short: Outline: three arguments proven via Lemmas 4.1 and 4.3.

nodes.statement:
[Arg. 1:] Denote $p_r = P_{\mathcal{M}}(r)$.
    Then, since $r - p_r\perp T_{p_r}\mathcal{M} $ and $r\in\mathcal{M}_\sigma$, we have that $q = p_r$ along with $H= T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}$ are in the search space defined by the constraints of \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean}.
nodes.name: Arg. 1: feasibility of $(p_r, T_{p_r}\mathcal{M})$
nodes.statement_short: The true projection and tangent lie in the search space.

nodes.statement:
[Arg. 2:] From Lemma \ref{lem:J1pTp_clean} it follows that for large enough $M = \tau/\sigma$ such that $ \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\tau}}  + \frac{\sigma}{\tau} < \frac{1}{2} $ we have $J_1(r; p_r; T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}) \leq 50\cdot \sigma^2$. 
    According to Assumption \ref{assume:noise} in Section \ref{sec:SamplingAssumptions}, we have that $M$ is large enough, and Lemma \ref{lem:J1pTp_clean} hold.
    Due to the definition of $q^*, H^*$ in \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean}, we achieve that $J_1(r; q^*, H^*) \leq 50 \cdot \sigma^2$ as well.
nodes.name: Arg. 2: small score of the minimizer
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 4.1 the tangent scores at most $50\sigma^2$, hence so does the minimizer.

nodes.statement:
[Arg. 3:] From Lemma \ref{lem:J_1qH_clean}, we have that  
    for $\alpha = \sqrt{C_M/M}$, where $M = \frac{\tau}{\sigma}$, and $C_M$ is a constant
    the following holds:
    For any $\delta >0$ arbitrarily small there is $ N_{\delta} $ sufficiently large (independent of $\alpha$) such that for all $ n>N_{\delta} $, \textbf{all} pairs $(q, H)$ in the search space of \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} such that $\angle_{max}(H,T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}) > \alpha$, the score $J_1(r; q, H) \geq 100 \sigma^2 $ with probability of at least $1 - \delta$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.name: Arg. 3: tilted planes score high
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 4.3 every plane tilted more than $\alpha$ scores at least $100\sigma^2$ w.h.p.

nodes.statement:
Combining Arguments 2 and 3 we have that 
for $\alpha = \sqrt{C_M/M}$, where $M = \frac{\tau}{\sigma}$, and $C_M$ is a constant
the following holds:
	For any $\delta>0$ arbitrarily small, there exists $ N_{\delta} $ (independent of $\alpha$) such that for all $ n > N_{\delta} $ 
	\[\angle_{\max}(H^*, T_p\mathcal{M})\leq \alpha\]
	with probability of at least $ 1 - \delta $. Additionally, since the search space of \eqref{eq:argmin1_clean} requires that $\|r-q^*\| <2\sigma$, we have that $\|p-q^*\|\leq 3\sigma$, and the proof is concluded.
nodes.name: Combine arguments
nodes.statement_short: Combine Args. 2 and 3 to bound the angle of $H^*$; the search region gives $\|p-q^*\|\le 3\sigma$.

Since $\angle(y_{	ilde j}, 	ilde y_{	ilde j}) = eta_{	ilde j} $ we can use the Euclidean geometry on $\mathcal{L}_{	ilde j}$ (Figure ef{fig:Lk_clean}) to get \[ \lrangle{q, 	ilde y_{	ilde j}} = \lrangle{q, 	extrm{Rot}( eta_{	ilde j}) y_{	ilde j}} = \lrangle{	extrm{Rot}(- eta_{	ilde j}) q, y_{	ilde j}} ,\] where $	extrm{Rot}(	heta)$ denotes the rotation matrix in $\mathbb{R}^D$ with respect to the angle $	heta$ in $\mathcal{L}_{	ilde j}$ . \left(	au-\sqrt{	au^2-\|q^{\vec{x}}\|^2} ight)\cos  eta_{	ilde j}} \ &\geq\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma	au}\sin  eta_{	ilde j} - 	au\left(1-\sqrt{1- (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/	au} ight)\cos  eta_{	ilde j} ight) \ &\geq	au\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/	au}\sin  eta_{	ilde j}-\cos  eta_{	ilde j} + \cos  eta_{	ilde j}(1- (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma /	au) ight) \ &= 	au \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/	au}\sin  eta_{	ilde j} -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/	au \cos eta_{	ilde j}ight) \ &\geq 	au \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/	au}\sin  eta_{	ilde j} -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/	au ight) ,\end{align*} and  egin{equation} |\langle q, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j} angle| \geq 	au \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/	au}\sin \alpha_0 -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/	au ight) .\end{equation} Since $\|	ilde{q} - q\| \leq \sigma $ we get $$\abs{\lrangle{	ilde q - q, 	ilde y_{	ilde j}}} = |\langle 	ilde{q}, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle - \langle q, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle| \leq\sigma,$$ and so,  egin{align*} |\langle q, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle| - |\langle 	ilde{q}, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle|&\leq |\langle q, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle - \langle 	ilde{q}, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle| \leq \sigma\ |\langle 	ilde{q}, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle|&\geq |\langle q, 	ilde{y}_{	ilde j}angle| - 4(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}	au^{1/2} + \sigma^2 \end{align*} Thus, by choosing for example $a_1 =  rac{1}{4}$ and $a_2 =  rac{1}{8}$ we get  egin{equation} \lrangle{	ilde q, 	ilde y_{	ilde j}}^2 \geq  rac{1}{64}\sigma 	au sin\alpha_0 - nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $J_1$ via principal angles into the tangent score plus $R_1=R_1'+R_1''$; bound $R_1''\ge -9\sigma^2$ and show many samples in a good region make $R_1'$ large. Key step: a ball in the ROI where $\langle r_i-p,\tilde y_j\rangle^2$ is large.

nodes.statement:
We first wish to denote by $\beta_j$ the principal angles between $H$ and $T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}$ and their matching principal pairs $(u_j, w_j)\in T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}\times H$ (see Definition \ref{def:principal_angles_clean}).  
Throughout the proof we work on the sectional planes defined by $\mathcal{L}_j = Span\{u_j,w_j\}$.
Thus, we can define the orthogonal complement of $u_j$ and $w_j$ on $\mathcal{L}_j$ by $y_j$ and $\tilde y_j$ correspondingly.
That is, both $\{u_j, y_j\}$ and $\{w_j, \tilde y_j\}$ are orthogonal bases of $\mathcal{L}_j$.
Since for any $i \neq j$ we have that $u_i \perp w_j$, $u_i \perp u_j$ and $w_i \perp w_j$, we have that both $\{\tilde y_j\}_{j=1}^{d}$ and $\{y_j\}_{j=1}^{d}$ are orthonormal sets.
Then, complete the sets $\{\tilde y_j\}_{j=1}^{d}$ and $\{y_j\}_{j=1}^{d}$  to an orthonormal basis of $H^\perp$  and $T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}^\perp$ through adding the orthonormal sets $\{\tilde y_j\}_{j=d+1}^{D-d}$ and $\{y_j\}_{j=d+1}^{D-d}$ correspondingly.
Explicitly, we know that for all $j' = 1\ldots, d$
$$\textrm{Span}\{\tilde y_j\}_{j=d+1}^{D-d}\perp \mathcal{L}_{j'} ~~,~~ \textrm{Span}\{ y_j\}_{j=d+1}^{D-d}\perp \mathcal{L}_{j'}.$$ 
Thus, for $j=d+1, \ldots, D-d$ we have both $\tilde y_j , y_j\in H^\perp \cap T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}^\perp$ and without limiting the generality we can choose $\tilde y_j = y_j$ for such $j$.
Using this notation we get that for any point $x\in U_\textrm{ROI}$
\[
\operatorname{dist}^2(x - {p_r}, H) = 
\sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \lrangle{x - {p_r}, \tilde y_j}^2 =
\sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \lrangle{x - {p_r}, \tilde y_j}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \left[\lrangle{x - {p_r},  y_j}^2 - \lrangle{x - {p_r},  y_j}^2\right] =
\]
\[
=\sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \lrangle{x - {p_r}, y_j}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{D-d}\left[ \lrangle{x - {p_r},  \tilde y_j}^2 - \lrangle{x - {p_r},  y_j}^2\right]
,\]
and since $\tilde y_j = y_j$ for $j=d+1,\ldots,D-d$ we have
\begin{align} \operatorname{dist}^2(x - {p_r}, H) &=
	\operatorname{dist}^2(x - {p_r}, T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M}) + \sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[ \langle x - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle x - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2\right]
.\end{align}

The remainder of the proof is achieved through the following set of claims:
\begin{enumerate}
nodes.name: Principal-angle bases and decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Set up principal pairs, orthonormal complements, and split $\operatorname{dist}^2(x-p_r,H)$ into tangent distance plus a correction.

Explicitly, we know that for all $j' = 1\ldots, d$

nodes.statement_short: Introduce principal pairs $(u_j,w_j)$, planes $\mathcal{L}_j$ and orthonormal complements $y_j,\tilde y_j$.

Using this notation we get that for any point $x\in U_\textrm{ROI}$
\[
\operatorname{dist}^2(x - {p_r}, H) = 
\sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \lrangle{x - {p_r}, \tilde y_j}^2 =
\sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \lrangle{x - {p_r}, \tilde y_j}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \left[\lrangle{x - {p_r},  y_j}^2 - \lrangle{x - {p_r},  y_j}^2\right] =
\]

=\sum_{j=1}^{D-d} \lrangle{x - {p_r}, y_j}^2 + \sum_{j=1}^{D-d}\left[ \lrangle{x - {p_r},  \tilde y_j}^2 - \lrangle{x - {p_r},  y_j}^2\right]
,\]

nodes.name: Distance decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the squared distance to $H$ as distance to the tangent plus a sum over $j\le d$.

nodes.statement: \operatorname{dist}^2(x - {p_r}, H) &= \operatorname{dist}^2(x - {p_r}, T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M}) + \sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[ \langle x - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle x - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2\right] .

nodes.label: eq:EJ_1_clean

nodes.statement:
From \eqref{eq:EJ_1_clean} it follows that
    \[J_1(r; {p_r}, H) =  J_1(r;{p_r},T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}) +  R_1(r;{p_r},H),\]
    where
    \begin{equation} R_1(r; {p_r}, H) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}}  \langle r_i - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2
    .\end{equation}
nodes.name: Claim 1: $J_1(r;p_r,H)=J_1(r;p_r,T_{p_r}\mathcal{M})+R_1$
nodes.statement_short: The tilted score equals the tangent score plus the correction $R_1$.

nodes.statement: R_1(r; {p_r}, H) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d} \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2 .
nodes.name: Equation (24) [eq:sum_k_clean]
nodes.label: eq:sum_k_clean

nodes.statement:
Thus, in order to bound $J_1(r; {p_r}, H)$ from below we can focus on bounding $R_1(r; {p_r}, H)$.
    We then consider separately two sets of indices $\mathcal{K}', \mathcal{K}''$ such that $\mathcal{K}' \cup \mathcal{K}'' = \{1,\ldots, d\}$, where for all $j\in \mathcal{K}'$ we have $\beta_j > \alpha$ and for all $j\in \mathcal{K}''$ we have $\beta_j\leq \alpha$.
    Notice that since $\angle_{max}(H, T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}) > \alpha$ we, get that $\mathcal{K}' \not = \emptyset$ and that $\#\mathcal{K}'' \leq d-1$.
    Writing this explicitly we get
    \begin{equation} R_1(r; {p_r}, H) = R_1'(r; {p_r}, H)  +  R_1''(r; {p_r}, H)
    \end{equation}
    where 
    \begin{equation} R_1'(r; {p_r}, H) = \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}'} \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}}  \langle r_i - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2
    ,\end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation} R_1''(r; {p_r}, H) = \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''} \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}}  \langle r_i - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2
    .\end{equation}
nodes.name: Split $R_1$ into $R_1'$ and $R_1''$
nodes.statement_short: Split indices by whether $\beta_j>\alpha$, giving $R_1=R_1'+R_1''$.

nodes.statement: R_1'(r; {p_r}, H) = \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}'} \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - {p_r}, \tilde{y}_j \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - {p_r}, {y}_j \rangle^2 ,

nodes.label: eq:R1pp_def_clean

nodes.statement:
We show in \ref{sec:proof_claim_R1pp_bound_clean} that
    \begin{equation} R_1''(r; {p_r}, H) \geq
    -9 \sigma^2
    .\end{equation}
nodes.name: Claim 3: $R_1''\ge -9\sigma^2$
nodes.statement_short: The correction over small-angle indices is at least $-9\sigma^2$.

nodes.statement: R_1''(r; {p_r}, H) \geq -9 \sigma^2 .
nodes.name: Equation (28) [eq:R1pp_bound_clean]
nodes.label: eq:R1pp_bound_clean

nodes.name: Claim 4: lower bound on $\langle r_i-p_r,\tilde y_j\rangle^2$ on a good ball

nodes.label: eq:ri_tyk_bound_clean

nodes.statement: R_1'(r; p, H) \geq &\frac{\mu_{max}}{\mu_{min} }\cdot\frac{1}{9} \left(\frac{1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}{ 8}\right)^d\cdot \left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma \tau sin\alpha - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right) -9 \sigma^2 ,

nodes.statement:
For clarity of presentation we wish to first prove Claim \ref{thm:claim_R1p_bound_clean} and only then show the correctness of the formula \eqref{eq:ri_tyk_bound_clean} presented in Claim 
\ref{thm:claim_ri_tyk_bound_clean}.
\paragraph*{Proof of Claim \ref{thm:claim_R1p_bound_clean}:}
For all $j\in \mathcal{K}'$ we have $\beta_j>\alpha$.
Let us assume that there is only one index $\tilde j$ in $\mathcal{K}'$ (otherwise we can treat each index separately and arrive at the same conclusion), then \eqref{eq:R1p_def_clean} can be rewritten as
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) = \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2
.\]
Thus, the only property which affect the score of $R_1'$ is the difference between the measurements $\langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2$ and $\langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2$, both on the 2D plane $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$.
Accordingly, using the bisector of $\angle(\tilde y_{\tilde  j}, y_{\tilde  j})$ and its orthogonal complement, we can split $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ into four regions $L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4$ (see Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}), where in two regions ($L_2$ and $L_4$ in Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}) $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}} \geq \lrangle{r_i - p, y_{\tilde j}}$ and in the other two regions ($L_1$ and $L_3$ in Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}) $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}} \leq \lrangle{r_i - p, y_{\tilde j}}$.
By denoting 
$$U_{bad} = \{r_i \in U_\textrm{ROI} ~|~ P_{\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}}(r_i - p)\in L_1 \cup L_3\},$$
and
$$U_{good} = \{r_i \in U_\textrm{ROI} ~|~ P_{\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}}(r_i - p)\in L_2 \cup L_4\}$$
we get that
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) = \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\left[\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}\left[  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2\right] + \sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{bad}} \left[ \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2\right]\right]
\]
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\left[\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2\right]
.\]
Similar to \eqref{eq:ri_yk_bound_s_square_clean}, 
\[
\frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 \leq 9 \sigma^2
,\]
and thus
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2
-9\sigma^2
.\]
Therefore, all we need to show is that given $n$ large enough, there are enough samples in $U_{good}$ for which the value $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2$ is large enough.
Using Lemma \ref{lem:num_of_samples_in_a_ball_clean}, as described in Claim \ref{thm:claim_useStochasticLemma}, since $U_\textrm{ROI}\subset B_D(P_{\mathcal{M}}(r), \sqrt{\sigma \tau}+\sigma)$, then for any $\delta$ there is $N$ large enough such that for all $n>N$  with probability of at least $1 - \delta$ 
\[
\#|U_\textrm{ROI}| < 3n\cdot\mu_{min}\cdot \mathrm{V}_{d}\cdot (\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^d 
.\]
Thus,
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{1}{3n\cdot\mu_{min}\cdot V\cdot ( \sqrt{\sigma\tau} +\sigma)^d }\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2
-9\sigma^2
.\]
Below in the proof of Claim \ref{thm:claim_ri_tyk_bound_clean} we show that \eqref{eq:ri_tyk_bound_clean} holds (the proof below is independent of the current one, but utilizes the notion of $U_{good}$ defined above).
Explicitly, for $ r_i \in U_{good} $
\begin{equation*}
\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_j}^2 \geq \frac{1}{64}\sigma \tau \sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2}
.\end{equation*}
Combining this with Lemma \ref{lem:num_of_samples_in_a_ball_clean} we get that for any $\delta$ there is $N$ large enough such that for all $n>N$  with probability of at least $1-\delta$
\begin{align*}
R_1'(r; p, H) 
&\geq 
\frac{\frac{n}{3}\cdot \mu_{max}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot(a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})^d}{3n\cdot\mu_{min}\cdot V\cdot ( \sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^d}\left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 -  \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9\sigma^2 \\
&=
\frac{ a_2^d\cdot\mu_{max}}{9\cdot\mu_{min}}\left(\frac{ 1}{1+\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}\right)^d\left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9 \sigma^2
.\end{align*}
Since $1/(1+x) \geq 1-x$ for sufficiently small $x$ we have that, for large enough $M$ of Assumption \ref{assume:noise}, of section \ref{sec:SamplingAssumptions},
\[
\left(\frac{ 1}{1+\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}\right)^d \leq (1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau})^d
\]
holds.
Thus, we have 
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{ a_2^d\cdot\mu_{max}}{9\cdot\mu_{min}}(1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau})^d\left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9 \sigma^2,
\]
Since $a_2 = 1/8$ we have 
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{ \mu_{max}}{\mu_{min}}\cdot\frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}{ 8}\right)^d \left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9 \sigma^2,
\]
as required.
\qed

\paragraph*{Proof of Claim \ref{thm:claim_R1p_bound_clean}:}
For all $j\in \mathcal{K}'$ we have $\beta_j>\alpha$.
Let us assume that there is only one index $\tilde j$ in $\mathcal{K}'$ (otherwise we can treat each index separately and arrive at the same conclusion), then \eqref{eq:R1p_def_clean} can be rewritten as
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) = \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2
.\]
Thus, the only property which affect the score of $R_1'$ is the difference between the measurements $\langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2$ and $\langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2$, both on the 2D plane $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$.
Accordingly, using the bisector of $\angle(\tilde y_{\tilde  j}, y_{\tilde  j})$ and its orthogonal complement, we can split $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ into four regions $L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4$ (see Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}), where in two regions ($L_2$ and $L_4$ in Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}) $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}} \geq \lrangle{r_i - p, y_{\tilde j}}$ and in the other two regions ($L_1$ and $L_3$ in Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}) $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}} \leq \lrangle{r_i - p, y_{\tilde j}}$.
By denoting 
$$U_{bad} = \{r_i \in U_\textrm{ROI} ~|~ P_{\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}}(r_i - p)\in L_1 \cup L_3\},$$
and
$$U_{good} = \{r_i \in U_\textrm{ROI} ~|~ P_{\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}}(r_i - p)\in L_2 \cup L_4\}$$
we get that
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) = \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\left[\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}\left[  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2\right] + \sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{bad}} \left[ \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2\right]\right]
\]
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\left[\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 - \sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2\right]
.\]
Similar to \eqref{eq:ri_yk_bound_s_square_clean}, 
\[
\frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - p, {y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 \leq 9 \sigma^2
,\]
and thus
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2
-9\sigma^2
.\]
Therefore, all we need to show is that given $n$ large enough, there are enough samples in $U_{good}$ for which the value $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2$ is large enough.
Using Lemma \ref{lem:num_of_samples_in_a_ball_clean}, as described in Claim \ref{thm:claim_useStochasticLemma}, since $U_\textrm{ROI}\subset B_D(P_{\mathcal{M}}(r), \sqrt{\sigma \tau}+\sigma)$, then for any $\delta$ there is $N$ large enough such that for all $n>N$  with probability of at least $1 - \delta$ 
\[
\#|U_\textrm{ROI}| < 3n\cdot\mu_{min}\cdot \mathrm{V}_{d}\cdot (\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^d 
.\]
Thus,
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{1}{3n\cdot\mu_{min}\cdot V\cdot ( \sqrt{\sigma\tau} +\sigma)^d }\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_{good}}  \langle r_i - p, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle^2
-9\sigma^2
.\]
Below in the proof of Claim \ref{thm:claim_ri_tyk_bound_clean} we show that \eqref{eq:ri_tyk_bound_clean} holds (the proof below is independent of the current one, but utilizes the notion of $U_{good}$ defined above).
Explicitly, for $ r_i \in U_{good} $
\begin{equation*}
\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_j}^2 \geq \frac{1}{64}\sigma \tau \sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2}
.\end{equation*}
Combining this with Lemma \ref{lem:num_of_samples_in_a_ball_clean} we get that for any $\delta$ there is $N$ large enough such that for all $n>N$  with probability of at least $1-\delta$
\begin{align*}
R_1'(r; p, H) 
&\geq 
\frac{\frac{n}{3}\cdot \mu_{max}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot(a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})^d}{3n\cdot\mu_{min}\cdot V\cdot ( \sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^d}\left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 -  \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9\sigma^2 \\
&=
\frac{ a_2^d\cdot\mu_{max}}{9\cdot\mu_{min}}\left(\frac{ 1}{1+\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}\right)^d\left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9 \sigma^2
.\end{align*}
Since $1/(1+x) \geq 1-x$ for sufficiently small $x$ we have that, for large enough $M$ of Assumption \ref{assume:noise}, of section \ref{sec:SamplingAssumptions},
\[
\left(\frac{ 1}{1+\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}\right)^d \leq (1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau})^d
\]
holds.
Thus, we have 
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{ a_2^d\cdot\mu_{max}}{9\cdot\mu_{min}}(1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau})^d\left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9 \sigma^2,
\]
Since $a_2 = 1/8$ we have 
\[
R_1'(r; p, H) \geq \frac{ \mu_{max}}{\mu_{min}}\cdot\frac{1}{9}\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}}{ 8}\right)^d \left(\frac{1}{64}\sigma\tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} \right)
-9 \sigma^2,
\]
as required.
\qed

\paragraph*{Proof of Claim \ref{thm:claim_ri_tyk_bound_clean}:}
As a result of Corollary \ref{cor:GraphOfFunctionTau_ROI}, $r_i \in U_\textrm{ROI}$ can be written as 
$$
r_i = \underbrace{p+(x_i, \phi_p(x_i))}_{p_i}+\varepsilon_i ,
$$
where $x_i=P_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(r_i - p)\in T_{p}\mathcal{M}$ and $\|\varepsilon_i\| \leq \sigma$.
Since 
$$ 
B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau}-\sigma ) \subset B_D(r, \sqrt{\sigma\tau}) = U_\textrm{ROI}
$$
(see the blue disc on $T_p\mathcal{M}$ in Figure \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean}), we look for a point $x_0\in T_p\mathcal{M}\cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ and a radius $\rho >0$ such that $\Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma\subset B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau} - \sigma)$, where
\begin{equation}
    \Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma \stackrel{\bigtriangleup}{=} \{x ~|~ dist(x, \Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}) < \sigma\}
,\end{equation}
where we remind that
\[
\Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)} = \{p + (x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} ~|~ x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)\}
.\]
Furthermore, we choose $x_0$ and $\rho$, such that $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2$ is large for any point $r_i\in\Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma$ (see Figure \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean} for an illustration).

For convenience, we denote by $q^y, q^x, q^{\vec x}$ the projections of $q\in \Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma$ onto $y_{\tilde j}$ (i.e., $T_p\mathcal{M}^\perp\cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$), $u_{\tilde j}$ (i.e., $T_p\mathcal{M}\cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$) and $T_p\mathcal{M}$ respectively.
Let $a_1, a_2<1$ and we define 
$$\rho = a_2 \cdot\sqrt{\sigma\tau},$$
and 
$$x_0 = (a_1\sqrt{\sigma\tau})\cdot u_{\tilde j}\in T_p\mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}.$$
That is, 
\[
\norm{p - x_0} = a_1 \cdot \sqrt{\sigma\tau}
.\]
In order to make sure that $\Gamma^\sigma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}\subset U_{\textrm{ROI}}$ we restrict the choice of $a_1, a_2$ such that
\begin{equation} \forall x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau}): \norm{p+(x,\phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} ~-~ p}
    + \sigma < \sqrt{\sigma\tau} - \sigma
,\end{equation}
We wish to reiterate that $U_\textrm{ROI} = \{r_i ~|~ \norm{r - r_i}\leq \sqrt{\sigma \tau}\}$ and so $U_\textrm{ROI}\subset B_D(r, \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$.
Furthermore, since $\norm{r - p}\leq \sigma$, we have $B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau} - \sigma)\subset  B_D(r, \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$.
Accordingly, all points $p+(x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}}$ for  $x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2 \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$ are within our region of interest even when moved $\sigma$ away from the manifold in some direction into $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ (in Fig. \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean}  $B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})$ is the orange disc and the projections of $p+(x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} + \varepsilon(x)$ onto $T_p\mathcal{M}$ are limited by the green disc containing the orange disc).
Using the calculations in Appendix \ref{subsec:simplification_app} we can use a simpler demand using $a_1$ and $a_2$, which ensures that the inequality \eqref{eq:a1a2_restriction_clean} is satisfied. The simplified requirement is
\begin{equation} (a_1+a_2)<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} -\frac{\sqrt{2\sigma}}{\sqrt{\tau}}
.\end{equation}

Let us now bound the value of $\lrangle{\tilde q - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2$ from below, for any $\tilde  q\in \Gamma^\sigma_{\phi_p,B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})}$.
Every such $\tilde  q$ can be written as
\[
\tilde q = q + \varepsilon
,\]
where $q\in \Gamma^0_{\phi_p,B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})}$, and so 
 \begin{equation} (a_1 - a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}  \leq \abs{q^x} \leq \|q^{\vec{x}}\| \leq \|p-x_0\|+a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau} = (a_1 + a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}   
.\end{equation}
From Lemma \ref{lem:f_bound_circle_clean} we get that
\[
\abs{\lrangle{q, y_{\tilde j}}} \leq \tau-\sqrt{\tau^2-\norm{q^{\vec{x}}}^2} 
.\]
Thus, 
\[
\abs{\langle \tilde{q}, y_{\tilde j} \rangle} = |\tilde{q}^y| \leq \tau+\sigma-\sqrt{\tau^2-\|q^{\vec{x}}\|^2}
,\]
and by plugging the right hand side of \eqref{eq:qxBound_clean} we get
\begin{align*}
\langle \tilde{q}, y_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 & \leq \left(\tau+ \sigma -\sqrt{\tau^2-(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma\tau}\right)^2
\\& =\tau^2 \left(1+ \sigma/\tau -\sqrt{1-(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau}\right)^2
\\&\leq \tau^2(1+\sigma/\tau -(1-(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau))^2
\\&= \tau^2 (\sigma/\tau +  (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau)^2
\\&=  \sigma^2(1 +  (a_1+a_2)^2)^2
\\&\leq 2\sigma^2
,\end{align*}
where the last inequality comes from \eqref{eq:a1a2_simplification_clean}.
Since $\angle(y_{\tilde j}, \tilde y_{\tilde j}) =\beta_{\tilde j} $ we can use the Euclidean geometry on $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ (Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}) to get
\[
\lrangle{q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}} = \lrangle{q, \textrm{Rot}(\beta_{\tilde j}) y_{\tilde j}} = \lrangle{\textrm{Rot}(-\beta_{\tilde j}) q,  y_{\tilde j}}
,\]
where $\textrm{Rot}(\theta)$ denotes the rotation matrix in $\mathbb{R}^D$ with respect to the angle $\theta$ in $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ .
Therefore,
$$|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle| \geq \abs{-|q^x|\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  + |q^y|\cos \beta_{\tilde j}} = \abs{|q^x|\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  - |q^y|\cos \beta_{\tilde j}}.$$
Using Lemma \ref{lem:f_bound_circle_clean} and \eqref{eq:qxBound_clean} as before we get
\begin{align*}
 |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle| &=\abs{  |q^x|\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  -  \left(\tau-\sqrt{\tau^2-\|q^{\vec{x}}\|^2} \right)\cos \beta_{\tilde j}}
 \\
 &\geq\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  -  \tau\left(1-\sqrt{1- (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau} \right)\cos \beta_{\tilde j} \right)
 \\
 &\geq\tau\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j}-\cos \beta_{\tilde j} + \cos \beta_{\tilde j}(1- (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma /\tau) \right)
 \\
 &= \tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j} -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau \cos\beta_{\tilde j}\right)
 \\
 &\geq \tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j} -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau \right) 
,\end{align*}
and
\begin{equation} |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle| \geq \tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau \right) 
.\end{equation}
Since 
$\|\tilde{q} - q\| \leq \sigma $
we get 
$$\abs{\lrangle{\tilde q - q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}} = |\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle - \langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| \leq\sigma,$$
and so,
\begin{align*}
|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| - |\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle|&\leq |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle - \langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| \leq  \sigma\\
|\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle|&\geq |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| - \sigma\\
\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2&\geq \langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2 - 2\sigma|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| + \sigma^2\\
\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2&\geq \langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2 - 2\sigma|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle|
.\end{align*}
 Substituting $\abs{\lrangle{q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}}$ with the bound from \eqref{eq:q_yk_prod_clean} we get
\begin{align*}
    \lrangle{\tilde q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2 & \geq \tau^2 \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -  (a_1+a_2)^2{\sigma/\tau}\right)^2 - 2\sigma\tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -  (a_1+a_2)^2{\sigma/\tau}\right) \\
    &\geq \tau^2\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -  {\sigma/\tau}\right)^2 - 2\sigma\tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0\right)\\
    &= \tau^2 \left((a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma/\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 2(a_1-a_2)(\sigma/\tau)^{3/2}\sin\alpha_0 + (\sigma/\tau)^2\right) -2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\sqrt{\tau} \sin \alpha_0 \\
    &\geq (a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2}\sin\alpha_0 + \sigma^2 -2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}{\tau}^{1/2} \\
    &= (a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} + \sigma^2 -2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}{\tau}^{1/2} \\
    &= (a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 4(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} + \sigma^2 
\end{align*}
Thus, by choosing for example $a_1 = \frac{1}{4}$ and $a_2 = \frac{1}{8}$ we get
\begin{equation}
    \lrangle{\tilde q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2 \geq \frac{1}{64}\sigma \tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2}
.\end{equation}

\paragraph*{Proof of Claim \ref{thm:claim_ri_tyk_bound_clean}:}
As a result of Corollary \ref{cor:GraphOfFunctionTau_ROI}, $r_i \in U_\textrm{ROI}$ can be written as 
$$
r_i = \underbrace{p+(x_i, \phi_p(x_i))}_{p_i}+\varepsilon_i ,
$$
where $x_i=P_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(r_i - p)\in T_{p}\mathcal{M}$ and $\|\varepsilon_i\| \leq \sigma$.
Since 
$$ 
B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau}-\sigma ) \subset B_D(r, \sqrt{\sigma\tau}) = U_\textrm{ROI}
$$
(see the blue disc on $T_p\mathcal{M}$ in Figure \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean}), we look for a point $x_0\in T_p\mathcal{M}\cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ and a radius $\rho >0$ such that $\Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma\subset B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau} - \sigma)$, where
\begin{equation}
    \Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma \stackrel{\bigtriangleup}{=} \{x ~|~ dist(x, \Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}) < \sigma\}
,\end{equation}
where we remind that
\[
\Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)} = \{p + (x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} ~|~ x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)\}
.\]
Furthermore, we choose $x_0$ and $\rho$, such that $\lrangle{r_i - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2$ is large for any point $r_i\in\Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma$ (see Figure \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean} for an illustration).

For convenience, we denote by $q^y, q^x, q^{\vec x}$ the projections of $q\in \Gamma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}^\sigma$ onto $y_{\tilde j}$ (i.e., $T_p\mathcal{M}^\perp\cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$), $u_{\tilde j}$ (i.e., $T_p\mathcal{M}\cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$) and $T_p\mathcal{M}$ respectively.
Let $a_1, a_2<1$ and we define 
$$\rho = a_2 \cdot\sqrt{\sigma\tau},$$
and 
$$x_0 = (a_1\sqrt{\sigma\tau})\cdot u_{\tilde j}\in T_p\mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}.$$
That is, 
\[
\norm{p - x_0} = a_1 \cdot \sqrt{\sigma\tau}
.\]
In order to make sure that $\Gamma^\sigma_{\phi_p, B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, \rho)}\subset U_{\textrm{ROI}}$ we restrict the choice of $a_1, a_2$ such that
\begin{equation} \forall x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau}): \norm{p+(x,\phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} ~-~ p}
    + \sigma < \sqrt{\sigma\tau} - \sigma
,\end{equation}
We wish to reiterate that $U_\textrm{ROI} = \{r_i ~|~ \norm{r - r_i}\leq \sqrt{\sigma \tau}\}$ and so $U_\textrm{ROI}\subset B_D(r, \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$.
Furthermore, since $\norm{r - p}\leq \sigma$, we have $B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau} - \sigma)\subset  B_D(r, \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$.
Accordingly, all points $p+(x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}}$ for  $x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2 \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$ are within our region of interest even when moved $\sigma$ away from the manifold in some direction into $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ (in Fig. \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean}  $B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})$ is the orange disc and the projections of $p+(x, \phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}} + \varepsilon(x)$ onto $T_p\mathcal{M}$ are limited by the green disc containing the orange disc).
Using the calculations in Appendix \ref{subsec:simplification_app} we can use a simpler demand using $a_1$ and $a_2$, which ensures that the inequality \eqref{eq:a1a2_restriction_clean} is satisfied. The simplified requirement is
\begin{equation} (a_1+a_2)<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} -\frac{\sqrt{2\sigma}}{\sqrt{\tau}}
.\end{equation}

Let us now bound the value of $\lrangle{\tilde q - p, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2$ from below, for any $\tilde  q\in \Gamma^\sigma_{\phi_p,B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})}$.
Every such $\tilde  q$ can be written as
\[
\tilde q = q + \varepsilon
,\]
where $q\in \Gamma^0_{\phi_p,B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau})}$, and so 
 \begin{equation} (a_1 - a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}  \leq \abs{q^x} \leq \|q^{\vec{x}}\| \leq \|p-x_0\|+a_2\sqrt{\sigma\tau} = (a_1 + a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}   
.\end{equation}
From Lemma \ref{lem:f_bound_circle_clean} we get that
\[
\abs{\lrangle{q, y_{\tilde j}}} \leq \tau-\sqrt{\tau^2-\norm{q^{\vec{x}}}^2} 
.\]
Thus, 
\[
\abs{\langle \tilde{q}, y_{\tilde j} \rangle} = |\tilde{q}^y| \leq \tau+\sigma-\sqrt{\tau^2-\|q^{\vec{x}}\|^2}
,\]
and by plugging the right hand side of \eqref{eq:qxBound_clean} we get
\begin{align*}
\langle \tilde{q}, y_{\tilde j} \rangle^2 & \leq \left(\tau+ \sigma -\sqrt{\tau^2-(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma\tau}\right)^2
\\& =\tau^2 \left(1+ \sigma/\tau -\sqrt{1-(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau}\right)^2
\\&\leq \tau^2(1+\sigma/\tau -(1-(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau))^2
\\&= \tau^2 (\sigma/\tau +  (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau)^2
\\&=  \sigma^2(1 +  (a_1+a_2)^2)^2
\\&\leq 2\sigma^2
,\end{align*}
where the last inequality comes from \eqref{eq:a1a2_simplification_clean}.
Since $\angle(y_{\tilde j}, \tilde y_{\tilde j}) =\beta_{\tilde j} $ we can use the Euclidean geometry on $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ (Figure \ref{fig:Lk_clean}) to get
\[
\lrangle{q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}} = \lrangle{q, \textrm{Rot}(\beta_{\tilde j}) y_{\tilde j}} = \lrangle{\textrm{Rot}(-\beta_{\tilde j}) q,  y_{\tilde j}}
,\]
where $\textrm{Rot}(\theta)$ denotes the rotation matrix in $\mathbb{R}^D$ with respect to the angle $\theta$ in $\mathcal{L}_{\tilde j}$ .
Therefore,
$$|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle| \geq \abs{-|q^x|\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  + |q^y|\cos \beta_{\tilde j}} = \abs{|q^x|\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  - |q^y|\cos \beta_{\tilde j}}.$$
Using Lemma \ref{lem:f_bound_circle_clean} and \eqref{eq:qxBound_clean} as before we get
\begin{align*}
 |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle| &=\abs{  |q^x|\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  -  \left(\tau-\sqrt{\tau^2-\|q^{\vec{x}}\|^2} \right)\cos \beta_{\tilde j}}
 \\
 &\geq\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j}  -  \tau\left(1-\sqrt{1- (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau} \right)\cos \beta_{\tilde j} \right)
 \\
 &\geq\tau\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j}-\cos \beta_{\tilde j} + \cos \beta_{\tilde j}(1- (a_1+a_2)^2\sigma /\tau) \right)
 \\
 &= \tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j} -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau \cos\beta_{\tilde j}\right)
 \\
 &\geq \tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \beta_{\tilde j} -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau \right) 
,\end{align*}
and
\begin{equation} |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j} \rangle| \geq \tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -(a_1+a_2)^2\sigma/\tau \right) 
.\end{equation}
Since 
$\|\tilde{q} - q\| \leq \sigma $
we get 
$$\abs{\lrangle{\tilde q - q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}} = |\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle - \langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| \leq\sigma,$$
and so,
\begin{align*}
|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| - |\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle|&\leq |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle - \langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| \leq  \sigma\\
|\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle|&\geq |\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| - \sigma\\
\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2&\geq \langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2 - 2\sigma|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle| + \sigma^2\\
\langle \tilde{q}, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2&\geq \langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle^2 - 2\sigma|\langle q, \tilde{y}_{\tilde j}\rangle|
.\end{align*}
 Substituting $\abs{\lrangle{q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}}$ with the bound from \eqref{eq:q_yk_prod_clean} we get
\begin{align*}
    \lrangle{\tilde q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2 & \geq \tau^2 \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -  (a_1+a_2)^2{\sigma/\tau}\right)^2 - 2\sigma\tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -  (a_1+a_2)^2{\sigma/\tau}\right) \\
    &\geq \tau^2\left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0 -  {\sigma/\tau}\right)^2 - 2\sigma\tau \left((a_1-a_2)\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}\sin \alpha_0\right)\\
    &= \tau^2 \left((a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma/\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 2(a_1-a_2)(\sigma/\tau)^{3/2}\sin\alpha_0 + (\sigma/\tau)^2\right) -2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\sqrt{\tau} \sin \alpha_0 \\
    &\geq (a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2}\sin\alpha_0 + \sigma^2 -2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}{\tau}^{1/2} \\
    &= (a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} + \sigma^2 -2(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}{\tau}^{1/2} \\
    &= (a_1-a_2)^2{\sigma\tau}\sin^2 \alpha_0 - 4(a_1-a_2)\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2} + \sigma^2 
\end{align*}
Thus, by choosing for example $a_1 = \frac{1}{4}$ and $a_2 = \frac{1}{8}$ we get
\begin{equation}
    \lrangle{\tilde q, \tilde y_{\tilde j}}^2 \geq \frac{1}{64}\sigma \tau sin\alpha_0 - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^{3/2}\tau^{1/2}
.\end{equation}

nodes.statement: Let $H_\ell\in Gr(d, D)$, and let $f_\ell:H_\ell\simeq\mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{D-d}$, defined as in \eqref{eq:fl_def}. Define $H_{\ell+1} = \mathrm{Im}(\mathcal{D}_{\pi^*_{q_\ell,H_{\ell}}}[0])$, as in Algorithm \ref{alg:step2_clean}. Let $f_{\ell+1/2}$ be as defined in \eqref{eq:fl12_def} and let $r_1 = \frac{k-1}{2k +d}$. Assume that $M = \frac{\tau}{\sigma} \geq C_\tau \sqrt{D\log D}$ (where $C_\tau$ is a constant from Lemma \ref{lem:Tf_TtildeF_D}). For any $\delta>0$, there is $N$ such that for any number of samples $n>N$, and any $\alpha \leq\frac{3}{2} \sqrt{C_M/M}$ smaller than some constant (see Theorem \ref{thm:Step1} and Section \ref{sec:SamplingAssumptions} for the definition of $M$ and $C_M$). If \begin{enumerate} \item $\angle_{\max} (H_\ell, T_0 f_\ell) = \alpha_\ell\leq \alpha$ \item $48\frac{\|f_\ell(0)\|}{\tau} \leq \alpha$ \item $ 12\sqrt{d} \frac{C_0 \ln(1/\delta)}{n^{r_1}}\leq \alpha $ \end{enumerate} hold, where $C_0$ is some constant. Then, we have \[ \alpha_{\ell+1} = \angle_{\max} (H_{\ell+1}, T_0 f_{\ell+1}) = \angle_{\max} (H_{\ell+1}, T_0 f_{\ell+1/2}) \leq \alpha/2 \] with probability at least $1-\delta$.

nodes.statement: We divide Algorithm \ref{alg:step2_clean} into three steps: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] Initialize $q_0$ and $H_0$ - corresponds to rows 3 and 4 in Algorithm \ref{alg:step2_clean}. \item[(ii)] Estimate $H_{\ell+1}$ from $H_{\ell}$ and $q_\ell$ - corresponds to rows 6 to 8 in Algorithm \ref{alg:step2_clean}. \item[(iii)] Estimate $q_{\ell+1}$ from $H_{\ell+1}$ - corresponds to row 10 in Algorithm \ref{alg:step2_clean}. \end{enumerate} Where steps (ii) and (iii) are repeated $\kappa$ times. We will treat the three steps one by one, and prove that the "output" of each step will fit our requirements for the input of the next step. Although we will prove this point later, we start with assuming that $\kappa$ and $\delta_1$ are such that \begin{equation} 12\sqrt{d}\frac{C_0 \ln(1/\delta_1)}{n^{r_1}} \leq \alpha_0 2^{-\kappa+1}, \end{equation} where $C_0$ is the constant from Lemma \ref{lem:main_support_theorem_step2}. We start with \textbf{step (i)}: From Lemma \ref{lem:Tf_Tftilde_Init} there is $N_{1,\delta_1}$ such that for all $n>N_{1,\delta_1}$ we have that: \[ \Pr\left(\angle_{\max} (T_0f_{0}, H_{0}) \leq \alpha_1 \right) \geq 1-\delta_1, \] where $\alpha_1 = \frac{3}{2} \alpha_0$. From Lemma \ref{lem:dist_to_f_l0_weak} Since $\alpha <1/D^{1/4}$ there is $N_{2,\delta_1}$ such that for all $n>N_{2,\delta_1}$ we have that: \[ \Pr\left(\|f_0(0)\| \leq \tau \alpha_1 /48\right) \geq 1-\delta_1 \] hold. Denote by $A_\ell$ the event that $\angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell}, H_{\ell}) \leq \alpha_1 2^{-\ell}$ and by $B_\ell$ the event that $\|f_\ell(0)\| \leq \tau \alpha_1 2^{-\ell} /48$, and then, by the union bound, we have that $\Pr(A_0 \mbox{ and } B_0) \geq 1-2\delta_1$. Next, considering \textbf{step(ii)}. Since $M>C_\tau \sqrt{D\log D}$, and $\alpha_1 \leq \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{ C_M/M}$ if events $A_\ell$ and $B_\ell$ hold, then, the requirements of Lemma \ref{lem:main_support_theorem_step2} are met for $\alpha = \alpha_1 2^{-\ell}$. Since $\angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell+1/2}, H_{\ell+1}) =\angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell+1}, H_{\ell+1}) $, we have that for $n> N_{3,\delta_1}$, with probability of at least $1-\delta_1$, the event $A_{\ell+1}$ holds, i.e \[ \Pr(A_{\ell+1}|A_\ell, B_\ell) \geq 1-\delta_1. \] For \textbf{step(iii)}, we show that given that the event $A_{\ell+1}$ holds, then, with probability of at least $1-\delta_1$, the event $B_{\ell+1}$ holds. From Lemma \ref{lem:dist_to_f_l0_weak} with $\alpha = \alpha_1 2^{-\ell}$ there is $N_{4,\delta_1}$ such that for all $n>N_{4,\delta_1}$ we have that: \[ \Pr\left(\|f_{\ell+1}(0)\| \leq \tau \alpha_1 2^{-(\ell+1)}/48\right) \geq 1-\delta_1 \] hold. To conclude our arguments so far, since $\kappa$ satisfies \eqref{eq:n_bound1}, using the union bound on the events $A_0,\ldots, A_\kappa$ and $B_0,\ldots, B_\kappa$ we have that \begin{equation} \Pr\left(\angle_{\max} (T_0 f_{\kappa}, H_{\kappa}) \leq \alpha_1 2^{-\kappa}\right) \geq 1 - 2\kappa\delta_1. \end{equation} Choosing $\delta_1 = \frac{\delta}{2\kappa}$, we have from Lemma \ref{lem:comute_kappa}, that $\kappa$ from \eqref{eq:kappa_res_lem} satisfies \eqref{eq:n_bound1_kappa_lem}, and thus $\kappa$ satisfies \eqref{eq:n_bound1} as well. We also have from Lemma \ref{lem:comute_kappa} that \[ \alpha_1 2^{-\kappa} \leq C_{d} \ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right) n^{-r_1}\left(\ln\left(\ln(n) \right)\right)^{2r_1}. \] Thus, we have that \begin{equation} \Pr\left(\angle_{\max} (Tf_{\kappa}(0), H_{\kappa}) \leq C_{d}\ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right) n^{-r_1}\left(\ln\left(\ln(n) \right)\right)^{2r_1}\right) \geq 1-\delta. \end{equation} This concludes the proof of Eq. \eqref{eq:thm3.3_tangent_ang}. Furthermore, assuming event $A_\kappa$ holds, there is $N_5$ such that for $n>N_{5}$ we have that $\alpha = \alpha_1 2^{-\kappa}<1/D$. Thus, from Lemma \ref{lem:dist_to_f_l0_srtong_small_alpha} we have that \[ \|f_\kappa(0)\| \leq DC_1 \alpha_1^2 2^{-2\kappa} + \frac{C_2\ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)}{n^{r_0}} \] holds with probability at least $1-\delta_1$. Denote this event by $\bar{B}_\kappa$. Substituting $\kappa$ from \eqref{eq:kappa_res_lem} we have from Lemma \ref{lem:comute_kappa} that \[ \| f_\kappa(0)\| \leq D C_1 C_{d}^2 \ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)^2 n^{-2r_1}\left(\ln\left(\ln(n) \right)\right)^{4r_1} + C_2\ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)n^{-r_0} \] or, for $n$ large enough, and some constant $C$, \[ \|f_\kappa(0)\| \leq C \ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right) n^{-r_0}. \] Thus, using the union bound on $A_1,\ldots, A_\kappa, B_1,\ldots, B_{\kappa-1}$, and $\bar{B}_\kappa$, we have that \begin{equation} \Pr\left( \|f_\kappa(0)\| \leq C\ln\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right) n^{-r_0} \right) \geq 1-\delta. \end{equation} This concludes the proof of Eq. \eqref{eq:thm3.3_p_bound} and of Theorem \ref{thm:Step2}.

 \[

nodes.statement: From Lemma \ref{lem:Tf_TtildeF_D} we have that \begin{equation} \angle_{\max}(T_0 f_\ell, T_0 {\wtilde{f}_\ell}) \leq \frac{\alpha}{6}. \end{equation} From Lemma \ref{lem:AngleImprovement} we have that for any $\delta$ and $n>N_{\delta}$, \[ \Pr(\angle_{\max}(T_0\wtilde f_\ell, T_0\pi^*_{q_0, H_\ell}) \geq 2\sqrt{d}\frac{C_0 \ln(1/\delta)}{n^{r_1}}) < \delta. \] Thus, as $ 12\sqrt{d} \frac{C_0 \ln(1/\delta)}{n^{r_1}}\leq \alpha $ (see assumption 3 in the lemma), we have \begin{equation} \Pr(\angle_{\max}(T_0\wtilde f_\ell, T_0\pi^*_{q_0, H_\ell}) \geq \frac{\alpha}{6}) < \delta. \end{equation} And, from \[ \angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell}, H_{\ell+1}) \leq \angle_{\max} (T_0f_\ell, T_0\wtilde{f}_\ell) + \angle_{\max} (T_0\wtilde{f}_\ell, H_{\ell+1}). \] along with \eqref{eq:bound_Tfl_Tftile_l} and \eqref{eq:pr_alpha_6}, we have that \begin{equation} \Pr\left(\angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell}, H_{\ell+1}) \geq \alpha/3\right) < \delta. \end{equation} In order to apply Lemma \ref{lem:shift_ang_general} we denote $g_0 = f_\ell$, $g_1 = f_{\ell+1/2}$, $G_0 = H_\ell$, and $G_1 = H_{\ell+1}$. Thus, we have that $\angle_{\max} (T_0g_0, G_0) = \angle_{\max} (T_0f_\ell, H_\ell)\leq \alpha$ and $\angle_{\max}(G_0,G_1) = \angle_{\max}(H_\ell,H_{\ell+1})\leq \angle_{\max}(H_\ell,T_0f_\ell) + \angle_{\max}(T_0f_\ell,H_{\ell+1})$. Under the assumption that the event described in \eqref{eq:pr_alpha_3} holds we also know that $\angle_{\max}(G_0,G_1) \leq \alpha + \alpha/3 = \beta$. Lastly, as $\alpha \leq \pi/16$, $\beta = \frac{4\alpha}{3} \leq \alpha_c$, and $\|f_\ell(0)\| \leq \frac{3\tau}{4 \cdot 16} $ (follows from assumption 2 of the lemma), we can use the result of Lemma \ref{lem:shift_ang_general} and obtain \[ \alpha_{\ell+1} = \angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell+1}, H_{\ell+1}) = \angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell+1/2}, H_{\ell+1}) \leq \angle_{\max}(T_0f_\ell,H_{\ell+1}) + \frac{ 8\|f_\ell(0)\|}{\tau} .\] Furthermore, since $\angle_{\max}(T_0f_\ell,H_{\ell+1}) \leq \alpha/3$ and $\frac{ 8\|f_\ell(0)\|}{\tau} \leq \alpha/6$, we have \[ \angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell+1}, H_\ell) = \angle_{\max} (T_0f_{\ell+1/2}, H_\ell) \leq \alpha/2 .\]

We assume that a point $x_0$ is chosen on the manifold and some direction $\vec v_0$ on the tangent $T_{x_0} \mathcal{M}$ (In practice, the process can initialized with a point near the manifold $\mathcal{M}$ and then project it to the manifold). 

The process of tracking a geodesic line is iterative. 
At each step, we compute $\wtilde x_{i+1} =  x_i + \varepsilon \vec{v}$, then ``project'' the new point back to the manifold $x_{i+1} \approx \mbox{Proj}_{\mathcal{M}} \wtilde x_{i+1}$ through Algorithms \ref{alg:step1Inpractice_clean} and \ref{alg:step2InPractice_clean}, and parallel transport $\vec v_i$ to $T_{x_{i+1}}$ to get $\vec v_{i+1}$.

nodes.statement:
In the first toy case, the manifold $\mathcal{M}$ is a circle of radius 10 in $\mathbb{R}^2$. 
The dataset consists of 5000 points. 
We start with some sample (illustrated in red in Figure \ref{fig:geoWalk_circle}), project it onto the circle (in Figure \ref{fig:geoWalk_circle}, the circle is marked in blue, and the projected point in green), and than move the point in some direction, project it again (shown in another green point in Figure \ref{fig:geoWalk_circle}), etc.
nodes.name: Geodesic walk on a circle
nodes.statement_short: Geodesic walk on a radius-10 circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$ from 5000 noisy points.

nodes.statement:
In the second example, we took a 3d model of an airplane\footnote{\textcolor{blue}{\href{http://3dmag.org/en/market/download/item/4740/}{http://3dmag.org/en/market/download/item/4740/}}}, rotated it in the z-axis, and took 2000 snapshots. Each snapshot is an image of $290 \times 209$ gray-scale pixels. The input data set consist of the unsorted images, sampled from a one dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{60,610}$.
Several such images appear in Figure \ref{fig:geoWalk_airplane}. 
Starting from some image, we create a movie of the rotating airplane. 
The movie can be found in \textcolor{blue}{\href{https://youtu.be/aHYyUvu1Q-8}{https://youtu.be/aHYyUvu1Q-8}}, and the code for generating it can be found in \textcolor{blue}{\href{https://github.com/aizeny/manapprox}{https://github.com/aizeny/manapprox}}

Then $\mathcal{M} \cap \emph{Cyl}_H(p,\rho, \tau/2)$ is locally a function over $H$, where $\emph{Cyl}_H(p,\rho, \tau/2)$ is the $D$-dimensional cylinder with the base $B_H(p, \rho)\subset H$ and height $\tau/2$ in any direction on $H^\perp$. Furthermore, $\rho = c_{\pi/4}\tau$ for some constant $c_{\pi/4}$. Explicitly, there exists a function $$ f:B_H(p, \rho) \to H^\perp $$ such that the graph of $f$ defined as $$ \Gamma_f = \{p + (x,f(x)) | x\in B_H(p, \rho) \} $$ identifies with $\mathcal{M} \cap \emph{Cyl}_H(p,\rho, \tau/2)$.

nodes.statement:
We split our arguments to two separate parts.
First, we show that for $c < 0.02$ there exists a function $f$ such that $\Gamma_f \subset M\cap \textrm{Cyl}_H(p,  c \tau, \tau/2)$.
Then, in the second part of the proof, we show that there is a constant $c_{\pi/4} < c$ such that $f$ is defined uniquely and $\Gamma_f = M\cap \textrm{Cyl}_H(p, \rho, \tau/2)$.

nodes.statement:
By definition, there is an open ball $U_T\subset T_p\mathcal{M}$ of $p$ such that there is a neighborhood $W_{\mathcal{M}} \subset \mathcal{M}$ that can be pronounced as a graph of a function from $U_T\simeq \mathbb{R}^d$ to $T_p\mathcal{M}^\perp\simeq \mathbb{R}^{D-d}$.
Accordingly, for any $H$ such that $\angle_{\max}(H, T_p\mathcal{M}) < \pi/2$ there is an open ball $B_H(p,\varepsilon) \subset H$ such that $W_H \subset \mathcal{M}$ can be pronounced as a graph of a function $f$  from $B_H(p,\varepsilon)$ to $H^\perp$.
We wish to show that $f$ can be extended to a ball $B_H(p, 0.02 \tau)\subset H$ such that the graph of $f$ is a subset of $\mathcal{M}$ (note that $f(0) = 0$).
nodes.name: Local graph exists
nodes.statement_short: Locally $\mathcal{M}$ is a graph over any non-orthogonal plane $H$.

nodes.statement:
By contradiction, let us assume that $\frak{r}$ the maximal radius of an open ball such that the $\Gamma_f \subset \mathcal{M}$, is strictly smaller than $0.02 \tau$.
We claim that the graph $\Gamma_f$ is defined on the closed ball $\bar B_H(p, \frak{r})$ and is also subset of $\mathcal{M}$.
This is true, from the following argument:
Take a sequence of points $\{x_n\}$ converging to $ x\in \partial \bar B_H(p, \frak{r})$, a point on the boundary of $\bar B_H(p, \rho)$, and consider $\{y_n = p + (x_n, f(x_n))\in \mathcal{M}\}$. From the compactness of $\mathcal{M}$ the sequence $y_n$ has a converging subsequence $y_{n_k}$ and we denote its limit as $y$.
Since $x_n \to x$, we define $f(x)\stackrel{\bigtriangleup}{=}\lim f(x_{n_k})$ and  $y = p + (x, f(x))$.

We now wish to show that there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that $f$ can be extended to $B_H(p, \frak{r} + \varepsilon)$.
Using a similar argument to the one used in the beginning of the proof, by showing that for any $x\in\partial B_H(p, \frak{r})$ the angle $\angle_{\max}(T_x f, H) < \pi/2$, we get that there is $W_H\subset\mathcal{M}$, a neighborhood of $y\in \mathcal{M}$ that is the image of some function from $B_H(x,\varepsilon_x)$ to $H^\perp$.
Therefore, $f$ can be extended into this neighborhood.
Taking $\varepsilon$ to be the minimum over all $\varepsilon_x$, which exists since $x$ is in $H(p, \frak{r})$, which is compact, we get that $f$ can be extended to $B_H(p, \frak{r}+ \varepsilon)$.

nodes.statement_short: Assume the maximal radius is below $0.02\tau$ and extend beyond it.

nodes.statement:
The remaining piece of the existence puzzle is showing that for all $x\in\partial B_H(p, \frak{r})$ we have $\angle_{\max}(T_x f, H) < \pi/2$.
From Lemma \ref{lem:alpha_beta_x_no_func} we have that for any $x$ such that 
\[
\frac{\pi}{2} > \frac{\pi}{4} + 2\sqrt{\frac{\norm{x}}{\tau}\left(2\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\norm{x}}{\tau}\right)},
\]
$\angle_{\max}(T_xf,H) <\pi/2$ holds.
Rewriting the inequality we get
\[
\begin{array}{cc}
      \\
    \frac{\pi}{4} > & 2\sqrt{\frac{\norm{x}}{\tau}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\norm{x}}{\tau}\right)} \\
    \frac{\pi^2}{8^2} > & \frac{\norm{x}}{\tau}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\norm{x}}{\tau}\right)\\
    0 > & \frac{\norm{x}^2}{\tau^2} + \frac{\pi}{2} \frac{\norm{x}}{\tau} - \frac{\pi^2}{8^2},\\
\end{array}
\]
and thus we require
\[
\frac{\norm{x}}{\tau} < \frac{-\frac{\pi}{2} + \sqrt{\frac{\pi^2}{4} + 4 \frac{\pi^2}{8^2} }}{2} = 
\pi \left(-\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{4}{8^2} }\right)
.\]
Finally, as 
$\pi \left(-\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{4}{8^2} }\right) >0.02$ we have that for $x<0.02\tau$,
$\angle_{\max}(T_xf,H) <\pi/2$ holds.

nodes.statement:
On the other hand, taking the point $(x, y_1)\in \mathcal{M}$, denoting $\beta = \angle_{\max} (T_{(x, y_1)}\mathcal{M}, H)$, and applying Lemma \ref{lem:alpha_beta_x_no_func} we have that
\[
\beta \leq
	\alpha + 2 \sqrt{ \bar x\lrbrackets{2 \alpha + \bar x} }
,\]
which tends to $\alpha$ when $\bar x\to 0$.
From Lemma \ref{lem:reach_ball_no_intersect_clean} we know that $(x,y_2)$ cannot be in any ball tangent to $\mathcal{M}$ at $(x, y_1)$ of radius $\tau$.
We denote by $v$ the direction $(0, y_2 - y_1)\in H^\perp$. 
From Lemma \ref{lem:angle_space_to_vec}  we know that there is $w \in \lrbrackets{ T_{(x, y_1)} \mathcal{M}} ^\perp$ such that $\angle (v, w) \leq \beta$.
Therefore, we can now limit our discussion to $L_{y_1}$ the affine space spanned by $v$ and $w$ from $(x, y_1)$, and note that it contains $(x, y_2)$ as well.
Taking the two balls $B_D((x, y_1) \pm \tau\cdot w, \tau)$ and intersecting them with $L_{y_1}$ we get two 2-dimensional disks of radius $\tau$ (see Figure \ref{fig:bouding_balls_for lem_locally_func}).
Thus, $(x, y_2)$ cannot be within either disks.
From basic trigonometry we achieve that either $y_2 = y_1$ or
\[
\norm{y_2 - y_1} \geq 2\tau\cos(\beta) \geq 2\tau\cos(\alpha + 2\sqrt{\bar x (2\alpha + \bar x)})
,\]
which tends to $2\tau \cos \alpha$ as $\bar x \to 0$.
Combining this with \eqref{eq:y2_y1_diff} we get there is $c_{\pi/4}$  such that for all $\bar x \leq c_{\pi/4}$ we have $y_1 = y_2$.

    \centering
    \includegraphics
 [width=0.5\textwidth]{Figures/BoundingCircle_Twicev2.pdf}
    \caption{Illustration of bounding balls. The reach $\tau$ of the manifold $\mathcal{M}$ (marked by the red line) bounds its sectional curvatures. Namely, the manifold cannot intersect a tangent ball of radius $\tau$. In this illustration we have some coordinate system $H$ and the manifold can be described locally as a graph of some function $f:H\to H^\perp$. The coordinate system $H$ is not aligned with $T_0f$, the tangent at zero; i.e., $\angle_{\max}(H, T_0f) = \alpha$. Then the value of $f$ at $x$ is bounded to the markered interval in $H^\perp$ above $x$. Furthermore, in order to have two different points in $\mathcal{M}$ above $x$, the manifold cannot curve too fast as it cannot enter neither the dotted balls nor the solid ones.} \end{figure}

nodes.statement: We recall that $ U_\textrm{ROI} $ as defined in \eqref{eq:ROI_clean} is contained in $ B_D({p_r}, \sqrt{\sigma\tau} + \sigma) $. Using Lemma \ref{lem:dist_ri_TpM_clean}, for any $r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}$ we know that the distance between $r_i - p_r$ and $ T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M} $ is bounded by \begin{equation} \operatorname{dist}(r_i - p_r,T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M}) \leq \tau-\sqrt{\tau^2-\|x_i\|^2} + \sigma ,\end{equation} where $ x_i = P_{T_{p_r}\mathcal{M}}(r_i - p_r) $. Since $ x_i \in B_D(0, \sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma )$ we have that $\norm{x_i} \leq \sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma $, and so \[ J_1(r; {p_r}, T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M}) \leq \left(\tau-\sqrt{\tau^2-(\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2} + \sigma\right)^2 .\] By simplifying and bounding this expression using Remark \ref{rem:taylor2_sqrt1-x2_clean} we get \begin{align*} \left((\sigma+\tau)-\sqrt{\tau^2-(\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2}\right)^2 = & (\sigma+\tau)^2 + \tau^2-(\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2 - 2(\sigma+\tau) \sqrt{\tau^2-(\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2}\\ = & \sigma^2 + 2\sigma\tau + 2 \tau^2 - (\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2 \\ &- 2\tau(\sigma+\tau) \sqrt{1-(\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2}\\ \leq & \sigma^2 + 2\sigma\tau + 2 \tau^2 - (\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2\\ & - 2\tau^2 (1-1/2 (\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2- (\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^4 )\\& - 2\tau\sigma (1-1/2 (\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2- (\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^4)\\ = & \sigma^2 - \tau^2(\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2 \\ & + \tau^2 ((\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2 +2(\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^4) \\& + \tau\sigma ((\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2+2(\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^4) \\ = & \sigma^2 + 2\tau^2 (\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^4\\& + \tau\sigma ( (\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^2 +2(\sqrt{\sigma/\tau}+\sigma/\tau)^4)\\ \leq & \sigma^2 + 2 \left(\sqrt{\sigma} + \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right)^4 + 3\sigma \left(\sqrt{\sigma} + \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right)^2 .\end{align*} Using the fact that $ \sigma \leq \tau $ we get \begin{align*} J_1(r; {p_r}, T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M}) &\leq \sigma^2 + 2(2\sqrt{\sigma})^4 + 3\sigma (2\sqrt{\sigma})^2 \end{align*} Thus, we obtain $$J_1(r; {p_r}, T_{{p_r}}\mathcal{M}) \leq 49 \sigma^2.$$
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1

nodes.statement: It is clear from \eqref{eq:R1pp_def_clean} that \[ R_1''(r; p, H) \geq - \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''} \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} \langle r_i - p, {y}_j \rangle^2 = - \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}}\sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''}\langle r_i - p, {y}_j \rangle^2 .\] Furthermore, since $y_j\in T_p\mathcal{M}^\perp$ and by Lemma \ref{lem:dist_ri_TpM_clean} we get \[ \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''}\abs{\lrangle{r_i - p, y_j}}^2 \leq dist^2(r_i - p, T_p\mathcal{M}) \leq \left(\tau - \sqrt{\tau^2 - \norm{P_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(r_i- p) }^2} + \sigma\right)^2 ,\] and since $r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI} \subset B_D(p, \sqrt{\sigma\tau} + \sigma)$ we get \begin{align*} \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''}\langle r_i - p,y_j \rangle^2 & \leq \left(\tau+\sigma-\sqrt{\tau^2-(\sqrt{\sigma\tau}+\sigma)^2}\right)^2 \\ & = \lrbrackets{\tau + \sigma - \tau\sqrt{1 - \lrbrackets{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\tau}} + \frac{\sigma}{\tau} }^2 }}^2 \end{align*} by Taylor expansion (Remark \ref{rem:taylor_sqrt1-x2_clean}) \begin{align*} \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''}\langle r_i - p,y_j \rangle^2 & \leq \lrbrackets{\tau + \sigma - \tau\lrbrackets{1 - \frac{1}{2}\lrbrackets{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\tau}} + \frac{\sigma}{\tau} }^2}}^2 \\ &= \lrbrackets{\sigma + \tau \frac{1}{2}\lrbrackets{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\tau}} + \frac{\sigma}{\tau} }^2}^2 \\ \end{align*} since $ \sigma < \tau $ we get $\sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\tau}} > \frac{\sigma}{\tau} $ and \begin{align} \sum\limits_{j\in\mathcal{K}''}\langle r_i - p,y_j \rangle^2 & \leq \lrbrackets{\sigma + 2\tau \frac{\sigma}{\tau}}^2 = 9 \sigma^2 \end{align} and \begin{equation*} R_1''(r; p, H) \geq - \frac{1}{\#|U_\textrm{ROI}|}\sum\limits_{r_i\in U_\textrm{ROI}} 9 \sigma^2 = -9 \sigma^2 \end{equation*}

nodes.statement:
We wish to rewrite the requirement of \eqref{eq:a1a2_restriction_clean} in terms of $a_1$ and $a_2$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:f_bound_circle_clean}, for all $x\in B_{T_p\mathcal{M}}(x_0, a_2 \sqrt{\sigma\tau})$:
\begin{equation*}
    \|\phi_p(x)\| \leq \tau - \sqrt{\tau^2 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma\tau}} 
;\end{equation*}
see Figure \ref{fig:ManifoldGoodDisc_clean}.
Thus,
\begin{align*}
\norm{(x,\phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}}}
& \leq \sqrt{(a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma\tau} + \left(\tau - \sqrt{\tau^2 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma\tau}}\right)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{(a_1+a_2)^2{\sigma\tau} + \tau^2 - 2\tau\sqrt{\tau^2 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma\tau}} + \tau^2 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma\tau}} \\
&= \sqrt{2\tau^2 - 2\tau^2\sqrt{1 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma/\tau}} } \\
&= \tau\sqrt{2} \sqrt{1 - \sqrt{1 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma/\tau}} } \\
&\leq \tau\sqrt{2} \sqrt{1 - (1 - (a_1+a_2)^2 {\sigma/\tau}) } \\
&= \sqrt{2}(a_1+a_2) \tau\sqrt{ {\sigma/\tau} } \\
&= \sqrt{2}(a_1+a_2) \sqrt{ {\sigma\tau} },\end{align*}
Where the second inequality results from applying \eqref{eq:Taylor2ndOrder}.
Therefore, the requirement of \eqref{eq:a1a2_restriction_clean} translates to
$$
\norm{(x,\phi_p(x))_{T_p\mathcal{M}}}_{T_p\mathcal{M},y_{\tilde j}}\leq \sqrt{2}(a_1+a_2)\sqrt{\sigma\tau}<\sqrt{\sigma\tau}-2\sigma
,$$
which can be simplified to 
$$
(a_1+a_2)<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \frac{\sqrt{2\sigma}}{\sqrt{\tau}} 
.$$
nodes.name: Simplification of the constraint on $a_1, a_2$
nodes.statement_short: Using Lemma 7.15 and a Taylor bound, the ROI containment requirement reduces to $a_1+a_2<1/\sqrt2-\sqrt{2\sigma/\tau}$.

u(x) \leq \mu_{\max}\mu(x)$. Suppose $X=\{x_j\}_{j=1}^n$ is a set of $n$ i.i.d. sample from $

For any $\varepsilon$, $\delta$ and radius $ho$, there is $N$, such that if $n>N$ the following holds: For any $x_0\in \Omega$ such that $B_d(x_0,ho)\subset \Omega$, we have \[ n( rac{\mu_{max}}{2}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdotho^d-\varepsilon) < \#|X \cap B_d(x_0, ho)| < n(2\cdot \mu_{min}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdotho^d+\varepsilon) \] with probability of at least $1-\delta$, where $\#|A|$ denotes the number of elements in the set $A$.

nodes.statement: Since $\Omega \subset B_d(0,R)\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists an $\tilde\varepsilon$-net (denoted by $\Xi$) such that \[ \#\abs{\Xi} = \ceil{ \frac{3R}{\tilde\varepsilon}}^d ,\] where $ \ceil{x} $ is the ceiling value of $ x $ \cite{vershynin2018high}. Around each point $p$ in $\Xi$, we consider a ball $B_d(p, (1 - \tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$. Note, that this $\tilde\varepsilon$-net along with these balls are independent of the choice of a specific ball $B_d(x_0,\rho)$. For each of the $B_d(p, (1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ , we consider our sample set as $n$ i.i.d random variables $Z^p_j$ which return the value $1$ if the sample lies within $B_d(p, (1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ and $0$ if not. Naturally, we get for all $j$ that \[ \Pr[z_j^p = 1] = \int\limits_{B_d(p, (1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)} d\nu \] Applying Hoeffding's inequality for each of the $B_d(p, (1 - \tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ we arrive at \begin{equation} \Pr[\overline{Z}^p - \mathbb{E}[\overline{Z}^p] \leq -\varepsilon] \leq e^{-2 n \varepsilon^2} , \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Pr[\overline{Z}^p - \mathbb{E}[\overline{Z}^p] \geq \varepsilon] \leq e^{-2 n \varepsilon^2} , \end{equation} where \[ \overline{Z}^p = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n Z_j^p. \] As a result \[ \mathbb{E}[\overline{Z}^p] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n\Pr[Z_j^p = 1] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n\int\limits_{B_d(p, (1 - \tilde\varepsilon)\rho)}d\nu ,\] and \begin{equation} \mu_{min} \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(B_d(p, (1 - \tilde\varepsilon)\rho)) \leq \mathbb{E}[\overline{Z}^p] \leq \mu_{max} \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(B_d(p, (1 - \tilde\varepsilon)\rho)) .\end{equation} Plugging this into \eqref{eq:HoeffingtonInequality1_clean} we get \begin{equation} \Pr\left[\overline{Z}^p - \mu_{max}\mathrm{Vol}\left(B_d(p, (1- \tilde\varepsilon)\rho)\right)\leq -\varepsilon\right] \leq e^{-2n \varepsilon^2} ,\end{equation} or, alternatively, since $\#|X \cap B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)| = n \cdot \overline{Z}^p$ we get \[ \Pr\left[\#|X \cap B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)| \leq n(\mu_{max}\mathrm{Vol}(B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho))-\varepsilon)\right]\leq e^{-2n \varepsilon^2} .\] Denoting by $A_p$ the event $\#|X \cap B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)| \leq n(\mu_{max}\mathrm{Vol}(B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho))-\varepsilon)$ we use the union bound to achieve \begin{equation} \Pr\left(\bigcup\limits_{p\in\Xi} A_p\right) \leq \sum\limits_{p\in\Xi} \Pr\left(A_p \right) \leq \ceil{ 3R/\tilde\varepsilon}^d \cdot e^{-2n \varepsilon^2} .\end{equation} Explicitly, the chances that there exists $B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ containing \textbf{less} sampled points than $n(\mu_{max}\mathrm{Vol}(B_d(p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho))-\varepsilon)$ are less than $c \cdot e^{-2n \varepsilon^2}$, where $c = \ceil{ 3R/\tilde\varepsilon}^d$. Going back to $B_d(x_0, \rho)$, we know that there exists a point $\tilde p\in \Xi$ such that \[ B_d(\tilde p,(1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)\subset B_d(x_0, \rho) .\] As a result, for any $\delta, \varepsilon, \rho$ there exists $N$ such that for all $n>N$ \[ \#|X \cap B_d(x_0, \rho)| > n(\mu_{max}\mathrm{Vol}(B_d((1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho))-\varepsilon) = n(\mu_{max}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot(1-\tilde\varepsilon)^d\rho^d-\varepsilon) ,\] with probability larger than $1-\delta$, where \[ \mathrm{V}_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)} .\] Similarly, instead of considering $B_d(p, (1-\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ we look at $B_d(p, (1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ for $p\in\Xi$ and alter the definitions of $Z^p$ accordingly. Then, by plugging the left inequality of \eqref{eq:EzBounds_clean} into \eqref{eq:HoeffingtonInequality2_clean} we get \[ \Pr[\overline{Z}^p - \mu_{min}\mathrm{Vol}(B_d((1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho))\geq \varepsilon] \leq e^{-2n\varepsilon^2} \] Utilizing the union bound once more we get the same bound as in \eqref{eq:UnionBoundAp_clean}. In other words, the chances that there exists a $B_d(p, (1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)$ containing \textbf{more} sampled points than $n(\mu_{min} \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(B_d((1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho)) + \varepsilon )$ are less than $\ceil{3R/\tilde\varepsilon}^d\cdot e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$. Going back to $B_d(x_0, \rho)$, we know that there exists a point $\tilde p\in \Xi$ such that \[ B_d(x_0, \rho) \subset B_d(\tilde p,(1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho) ,\] and for $\tilde\varepsilon$ small enough \[ B_d(\tilde p,(1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho) \subset \Omega .\] As a result, for any $\delta, \varepsilon, \rho$ there exists $N$ such that for all $n>N$ \[ \#|X \cap B_d(x_0, \rho)| < n(\mu_{min}\mathrm{Vol}(B_d((1+\tilde\varepsilon)\rho))+\varepsilon) = n(\mu_{min}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot(1+\tilde\varepsilon)^d\rho^d+\varepsilon) ,\] with probability larger than $1-\delta$. Finally, we get that for any $\delta, \varepsilon, \rho$ there exists $N$ large enough such that if $n>N$ we get \[ n(\mu_{max}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot(1-\tilde\varepsilon)^d\rho^d-\varepsilon) < \#|X \cap B_d(x_0, \rho)| < n(\mu_{min}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot(1+\tilde\varepsilon)^d\rho^d+\varepsilon) \] Since this is true for any $\tilde\varepsilon$, $(1+1/a)^a \leq 3$ and $(1-1/a)^a \geq 0.25$ we can choose $\tilde\varepsilon = \frac{1}{c_1 d}$ such that \[(1 - \tilde\varepsilon)^d \geq 0.25^{1/c_1} \geq 0.5,\] and \[(1 + \tilde\varepsilon)^d \leq 3^{1/c_1} \leq 2,\] and achieve \[ n(\frac{\mu_{max}}{2}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot\rho^d-\varepsilon) < \#|X \cap B_d(x_0, \rho)| < n(2\cdot \mu_{min}\cdot \mathrm{V}_d \cdot\rho^d+\varepsilon) \]
